name: Case-Based Reasoning Meets Large Language Models: A Research Manifesto For Open Challenges and Research Directions (Bach, Bergmann, Wiratunga et al.) [NOTE: the task title used the shorthand 'A Research Directions Roadmap'; the paper's actual subtitle is 'A Research Manifesto For Open Challenges and Research Directions'.]
venue: Working paper / preprint, deposited on HAL as hal-05006761v1 (deposited 26 Mar 2025). Authored collaboratively by the CBR-LLM research community and circulated/discussed at the 2nd Workshop on Case-Based Reasoning and Large Language Model Synergies (CBR-LLM) co-located with ICCBR 2025 (30 June 2025, Biarritz, France). It is explicitly cited as a 'Working Paper' (e.g. by Springer's LLsiM chapter) and is NOT one of the 30 peer-reviewed full papers in the formal ICCBR 2025 LNCS proceedings (LNCS vol. 15662, Springer); it is an ICCBR-adjacent community manifesto. [uncertain] whether it has since been formally published in a peer-reviewed venue.
authors_affiliation: 16 authors listed in alphabetical order with equal contribution; corresponding author Lukas Malburg (malburgl@uni-trier.de). Kerstin Bach (Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Trondheim, Norway); Ralph Bergmann, Florian Brand, Lukas Malburg (University of Trier & German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence (DFKI), Germany); Marta Caro-Martinez (cited as a CBR/XAI researcher, Spain); Viktor Eisenstadt (DFKI, Smart Data & Knowledge Services, Kaiserslautern, Germany); Michael W. Floyd (Knexus Research LLC, National Harbor, MD, USA); Lasal Jayawardena, Nirmalie Wiratunga (School of Computing, Engineering and Technology, Robert Gordon University, Aberdeen, UK); David Leake, Kaitlynne Wilkerson, Brian Schack (Luddy School of Informatics, Computing, and Engineering, Indiana University, Bloomington, IN, USA); Mirko Lenz (University of Trier & DFKI, Germany); David H. Menager (AI and Autonomy Group, Parallax Advanced Research, Beavercreek, OH, USA); Mirjam Minor (Department of Computer Science, Goethe University, Frankfurt am Main, Germany); Ian Watson (School of Computer Science, University of Auckland, New Zealand).
paper_url: https://hal.science/hal-05006761v1 (canonical HAL deposit; PDF at https://hal.science/hal-05006761v1/file/main.pdf). Author-hosted copy: https://www.mirkolenz.com/assets/Bach2025CaseBasedReasoningMeets.KHCYdg9G.pdf. Semantic Scholar CorpusId:282717922.
code_url: N/A (a position/manifesto paper; no method implementation or code release). It references concrete companion systems that have code, notably CBR-RAG (https://github.com/rgu-iit-bt/cbr-for-legal-rag).
maintained_repo_url: N/A (no maintained paper list / leaderboard accompanies this manifesto). Related community venue: the recurring CBR-LLM workshop proceedings on CEUR-WS (e.g. ICCBR 2025 CBR-LLM workshop, CEUR-WS Vol-3993).
task_domain: Cross-cutting position / roadmap spanning many task domains rather than one. The manifesto surveys the synergy of Case-Based Reasoning (CBR) and LLMs across QA (legal/medical/numerical reasoning QA), planning (case-based planning, agentic workflows), tool/agent use (supervisory multi-agent CBR-LLM roles), explainability/XAI, knowledge engineering, and decision-making. It is framed around CBR's four knowledge containers (vocabulary, similarity, case base, adaptation) mapped onto LLM mechanisms (episodic memory, case-based RAG, case-based planning).
problem_setting: A position / research-manifesto / roadmap paper (not a method and not an empirical study). It synthesizes a comprehensive literature review plus author expertise to (1) identify 13 open challenges grouped into four thematic areas (Guided Generation; Accuracy & Dehallucination; Explainability & Trust; Operational Efficiency) afflicting LLMs and CBR systems, and (2) propose 17 research directions/opportunities for combining CBR and LLMs bidirectionally (CBR-for-LLM and LLM-for-CBR). The setting discussed ranges across offline knowledge-engineering and interactive/agentic deployments, single- and multi-agent (supervisory agent roles), with no fixed supervision regime; the paper proposes directions rather than committing to one experimental setting.
what_is_retrieved: Cases (problem-solution episodes) are the central retrieved unit in the CBR view, used to enrich LLM prompts via case-based RAG. The manifesto also discusses retrieving/leveraging the four CBR knowledge containers: vocabulary, similarity knowledge, the case base, and adaptation knowledge; plus episodic memories (past prompts and their completions), guidelines/best practices stored as cases, and structured representations (workflows, graphs, plans). It contrasts these with generic docs retrieved by standard RAG.
retrieval_grounding: HYBRID as discussed. The classic CBR case base is treated as a curated/maintained store (which LLMs can also help acquire and maintain), while the manifesto promotes case-based episodic MEMORY that the system writes to over time (prompts and their completions as cases) and case-based RAG over a structured case base. So the proposed grounding spans a static/curated case corpus and a growing episodic memory, rather than a single fixed external corpus.
completeness_vs_topk_objective: Not formalized (no method, no fixed objective). Conceptually the manifesto favors precision/specificity over raw top-k: it argues standard RAG retrieval is too broad/generic and proposes multi-level (local fact + global context) case comparison and efficient case selection of 'critical facts' to fit limited context windows -- i.e. a precision-driven, context-budget-aware selection rather than a fixed top-k ranking or an explicit completeness objective. [uncertain] exact objective since this is a roadmap.
cbr_cycle_coverage: ['Retrieve', 'Reuse', 'Revise', 'Retain'] -- the full canonical 4R cycle is discussed (the paper repeatedly references the '4R cycle' of CBR1). As a manifesto it does not implement the cycle but proposes LLM roles across all four phases: Retrieve (case-based RAG, LLMs in the retrieval step), Reuse/Revise (adaptation rules/cases, LLM-prompted adaptation, supervisory adaptation advisors), and Retain (continuously updating the case base, LLM-assisted maintenance/curation).
explicit_cbr_grounding: true. The paper is authored by core CBR researchers and is explicitly and centrally grounded in case-based reasoning: it cites Aamodt & Plaza 1994 (ref 1), Richter's knowledge containers (refs 26-27), Schank's Dynamic Memory Theory / MOPs (ref 29), Kolodner-lineage CBR, Hammond's case-based planning (ref 10), and Watson 1999 'CBR is a methodology not a technology' (ref 33). CBR's 4R cycle and four knowledge containers are the organizing frame of the entire manifesto.
retrieval_unit: case (problem-solution episode) is the primary unit. The manifesto explicitly notes case representation formalisms range from plain text and attribute-value pairs to structured forms such as workflows, graphs, and plans. Other discussed units: episodic-memory items (prompt + completion), guideline/best-practice cases, vocabulary/domain-knowledge elements, similarity knowledge, and adaptation rules/cases. Cases are compared at multiple levels (local individual facts vs global overall context).
index_source: Mixed/hybrid as proposed: a curated case base (whose construction the manifesto proposes to accelerate via LLM-based knowledge acquisition to address the cold-start problem) plus a growing/online episodic memory of past prompts-and-completions that the system accrues. No single fixed offline-vs-online commitment is made; it is a roadmap advocating both maintained and self-growing case stores.
index_structure_topology: Discussed as structured/hierarchical and graph-capable rather than flat-only. The manifesto highlights structured case representations (workflows, graphs, plans), Schank's hierarchically organized Memory Organization Packages (MOPs) that index cases across multiple contexts and are assembled dynamically, taxonomy/knowledge-graph-derived similarity, and embedding-based (vector) similarity as one special form among many. So it spans flat vector indices, taxonomy/KG-backed indices, and hierarchical MOP-style memory organization.
retriever_type: Discussed as a spectrum centered on CBR similarity functions, not a single retriever. Embedding-based (dense) similarity is called out as one special form, complemented by classical CBR similarity measures (Euclidean distance, symbolic value tables, graph/text edit distances) and taxonomy/knowledge-graph-derived similarity. CBR-RAG (the cited concrete instance) uses general and domain-specific embeddings (BERT/LegalBERT/AnglEBERT) with inter/intra/hybrid similarity. LLMs are also proposed as agents in the retrieval step (LLM-as-retriever / fact weighting).
retriever_learning_signal: No retriever is trained in this paper (it is a manifesto). It surveys/proposes signals: classical CBR similarity is largely knowledge-engineered (manually defined measures), off-the-shelf embeddings are used in CBR-RAG, and the manifesto proposes LLM-assisted refinement of similarity measures -- learning latent features from past cases, dynamically revising attribute weights based on context, and integrating structured + unstructured descriptions. So proposed signals span none/off-the-shelf, knowledge-engineered, and LLM-feedback-driven similarity adaptation; no contrastive/RL retriever training is implemented.
query_construction: Discussed conceptually: in case-based RAG the structured case (its containers) is used to enrich/augment the LLM prompt, providing a richer query than the raw input (CBR-RAG augments the original query with contextually relevant cases). The manifesto also proposes filling prompt templates with case data via episodic memory, and using LLMs to extract/weight the relevant facts to retrieve (fact-weighting). No single query-construction algorithm is specified.
query_granularity: Discussed at multiple levels rather than fixed. Prompt-level (task) query augmentation via case-based RAG, multi-level comparison (local individual facts and global overall context), and step-level reasoning support via case-based planning / process-oriented CBR workflows that formalize sequential LLM calls. As a roadmap it does not commit to one granularity.
when_to_retrieve: Discussed as both one-shot (case-based RAG augmenting the prompt before generation) and iterative/adaptive (iterative RAG-style filtering, augmentation and refinement, where CBR is proposed to decide the optimal number of refinement iterations via abort conditions or similarity thresholds, and adaptive retrieval pipelines that adjust similarity thresholds). No single trigger regime is implemented.
retrieval_trigger_signal: Not implemented; proposed signals include CBR-style similarity thresholds and abort conditions to decide how many RAG refinement iterations to run, and dynamic adjustment of similarity thresholds in adaptive retrieval pipelines. The manifesto frames CBR as a controller that can govern WHEN to stop/continue iterative retrieval, but specifies no concrete trained trigger (token confidence, reflection tokens, etc.). [uncertain] beyond these conceptual proposals.
reranking: Not a focus / not implemented. The manifesto instead emphasizes multi-level (local vs global) case comparison and structured similarity for relevance/precision, and proposes supervisory LLM agents acting as reviewers; it does not specify a concrete cross-encoder/RRF reranking stage. [uncertain] (roadmap, no pipeline).
retrieved_context_refinement: Discussed conceptually under 'Reasoning for Filtering, Augmentation, and Refinement' (O2.3): CBR-LLM methods to filter, augment, and refine iterative-RAG context, using case-based planning to decompose generation tasks and compose results, LLMs as candidate plan generators that a case-based planner reviews/filters/augments, and CBR-controlled iteration counts. Structured case knowledge is proposed to validate and ground outputs (de-hallucination). No single refinement operator is fixed.
tool_document_engineering: N/A (the manifesto is about case/knowledge retrieval, not tool/skill-description engineering for a tool index). It does discuss serialization of structured case knowledge (e.g. JSON/XML) into prompts and the resulting context-size/cost tradeoffs (Challenge C2), but not tool-docstring augmentation.
index_content_separation: Not explicitly framed as progressive disclosure, but related ideas appear: C2 warns that serializing structured cases (JSON/XML) bloats the context window and cost, and O5.4 proposes efficient case selection that extracts only 'critical facts' from large case bases to operate within limited context windows -- a lightweight-selection-then-load pattern in spirit. [uncertain] (no concrete index/content split mechanism).
dynamic_index_and_protocol: N/A (no tool index / API protocol; not a tool-retrieval system). It mentions agentic workflows and supervisory multi-agent roles conceptually but specifies no RapidAPI/REST/MCP/function-calling integration.
tool_dependency_awareness: N/A (no inter-tool dependency modeling; the paper concerns CBR cases and knowledge containers, not tool dependency graphs).
how_retrieved_used: Primarily prompt augmentation / case adaptation. Retrieved structured cases enrich the LLM prompt with context-specific details (case-based RAG), grounding generation in verifiable evidence to reduce hallucination; the case container structure is reused to help the LLM produce more robust, well-structured answers. The manifesto also proposes case reuse with LLM-assisted adaptation (adaptation rules/cases), and a training-signal use: fine-tuning LLMs on structured cases (e.g. for JSON-schema-conformant structured outputs) and case-based distillation of LLMs.
planning_integration: Discussed prominently as retrieve/plan integration directions: case-based planning to guide the LLM reasoning chain (decompose a generation task, compose results following a case-based plan), LLMs as candidate plan generators inside a case-based planner that reviews/filters/augments, and process-oriented CBR (POCBR) representing sequential LLM calls as a workflow that formalizes system-LLM interactions (linked to 'agentic workflows'). It cites Hammond's case-based planning (ref 10), Bergmann et al. CBR-applied-to-planning (ref 3), Munoz-Avila & Cox case-based plan adaptation (ref 23), and the LLM-Modulo framing. No concrete MCTS/tree-search integration is implemented.
reasoning_search_interleaving_granularit: Discussed at the per-step / per-iteration and workflow level (decompose-then-compose under a case-based plan; CBR-controlled iteration counts in RAG refinement; POCBR workflows formalizing sequential LLM calls) as well as per-answer (one-shot case-based RAG augmentation). Not fixed to one granularity; a roadmap rather than a concrete interleaving schedule.
adaptation_mechanism: Discussed (CBR Reuse/Revise): the manifesto proposes LLM-prompted adaptation (LLMs propose adaptation rules or adaptation cases), supervisory LLM agents in roles such as output generators, reviewers, and adaptation advisors, and notes that plain prompt-instruction adaptation gave low accuracy in a classification scenario (citing Wilkerson & Leake, ref 34) -- motivating structured/knowledge-guided adaptation. It also proposes LLMs to refine adaptation strategies during maintenance. Spans LLM-prompted adaptation, critic/reviewer-guided revision, and adaptation-rule learning; nothing is implemented here.
retrieved_item_representation: Structured cases injected as context: structured case knowledge (attribute-value pairs, workflows, graphs, plans) and the case-container structure are surfaced to the LLM to produce robust, well-structured (e.g. schema-conformant) outputs; cases can also be turned into human-readable unstructured text by the LLM (O6.3). So both structured-note and raw/free-text representations are discussed, with emphasis on structured case knowledge for grounding and de-hallucination.
abstraction_level_of_retrieved_unit: Discussed across abstraction levels: concrete past cases (problem-solution episodes / examples), distilled guidelines/best-practices stored as cases, structured procedural knowledge (workflows, plans via case-based planning and POCBR), adaptation rules/cases, and episodic memories of prior prompts+completions. The manifesto spans raw-case, distilled-guideline, and reusable-workflow/plan abstractions.
noise_robustness_mechanism: Discussed conceptually: structured case knowledge and the four knowledge containers are proposed to validate outputs and reduce hallucination (de-hallucination through structured knowledge, O3.2), structured outputs enable correctness checking, evidence-based fine-grained retrieval grounds answers in real cases/factual data (O3.3), and supervisory reviewer/adaptation-advisor agents check generations. No trained noise-robustness mechanism is implemented (roadmap).
memory_type: Episodic (the paper's primary lens). It argues episodic memory is 'the missing piece' for long-term LLM agents (citing Pink et al. 2025, ref 24) and that episodic memory is the primary focus of CBR; it grounds this in Schank's Dynamic Memory Theory and hierarchical MOPs. Also discusses procedural/long-term memory and case-based long-term memory (LTM). So: episodic + (CBR) case-library / skill-and-workflow memory.
write_back: true (proposed). The manifesto advocates storing experiences as cases and continuously updating the case base; e.g. episodic memory of prompts and their completions, retaining best practices/lessons as cases, and LLM-assisted continuous case-base updating during the Retain phase. As a roadmap it proposes write-back rather than benchmarking a specific implementation.
online_growth: true (proposed). It promotes case-based episodic memory that accrues over time (prompts+completions), continuous case-base updating, and dynamic MOP-style memory whose structures change to reflect new understanding -- i.e. a store that grows/evolves during use rather than a frozen offline index.
write_back_trigger: Not formalized; the manifesto's Retain-phase proposals imply writing back successful/best-practice experiences and lessons (valid and best practices stored as cases) and continuously updating the case base, potentially with human-validated curation and LLM-assisted maintenance. Schank's dynamic memory implies write/update tied to understanding/learning events. No concrete on-success-vs-failure trigger is specified. [uncertain] (roadmap).
failure_experience_usage: Not specifically prescribed. The manifesto frames CBR as storing and reusing past experiences and 'lessons such as valid and best practices' (success-oriented), and proposes supervisory reviewer agents and validation to catch errors; it does not commit to a success-vs-failure contrastive memory scheme. [uncertain] whether failed experiences are explicitly stored/retrieved.
memory_evolution_update: Discussed conceptually via Schank's Dynamic Memory Theory: memory structures (MOPs) and the memories they reconstruct can change to reflect new understanding, and learning can change a MOP used later to assemble a memory -- i.e. link-and-evolve / refine dynamics. Also proposes continuous case-base updating, refining similarity assessments, and enhancing adaptation strategies (maintenance). Concrete mutation policy (append vs dedup-merge vs prune) is not specified.
retrieval_as_learned_policy: No (not implemented; no learned/RL case-selection policy). Retrieval is grounded in CBR similarity functions (largely knowledge-engineered or embedding-based). The manifesto proposes LLM-assisted refinement of similarity measures and adaptive similarity thresholds, but does not frame retrieval as an M-MDP / RL-optimized policy. [uncertain] only insofar as it is a forward-looking roadmap.
cross_agent_or_cross_framework_sharing: Touched conceptually: the manifesto envisions multi-agent / supervisory CBR-LLM systems with agents in distinct roles (output generators, reviewers, adaptation advisors), references MetaGPT (ref 12) and agentic-workflow/agent surveys (refs 31-32), and the iSee platform for defining, sharing, and reusing explanation experiences. So shared/reusable experience across roles/agents is discussed, but no concrete cross-framework memory-sharing protocol is implemented.
benchmarks: N/A -- no benchmarks are run (this is a position/manifesto paper with no experiments). It references empirical results from companion works it cites (e.g. CBR-RAG on legal QA; Wilkerson & Leake on implementing CBR with LLMs; Brand et al. LLMs as Knowledge Engineers; DS-Agent), but reports no datasets/environments of its own.
benchmark_family: N/A (no benchmark family; no empirical evaluation). The application domains discussed map loosely to QA (legal/medical/numerical reasoning), planning, XAI/explanation, and knowledge engineering, but the paper itself evaluates nothing.
baselines: N/A (no method, no head-to-head comparison). Conceptually it positions hybrid CBR+LLM systems against (a) standalone LLMs (which lack long-term memory, are opaque, and hallucinate) and (b) standalone classical CBR systems (which suffer the knowledge-acquisition bottleneck, cold-start, and limited algorithm transferability), and against plain RAG (argued less precise than case-based RAG).
key_metrics: N/A (no metrics reported -- no experiments). The paper's 'deliverables' are qualitative: 13 open challenges, 17 research directions/opportunities, and 4 thematic research areas (summarized in Table 1 mapping each challenge to its proposed research directions).
headline_result: N/A (no experimental headline). The headline contribution is the first systematic analysis of challenges and opportunities for bidirectional CBR-LLM integration: 13 open challenges grouped into 4 thematic areas (Guided Generation; Accuracy & Dehallucination; Explainability & Trust; Operational Efficiency) and 17 research directions, organized around mapping CBR's four knowledge containers (vocabulary, similarity, case base, adaptation) and the 4R cycle onto LLM mechanisms (episodic memory, case-based RAG, case-based planning, structured-output de-hallucination).
ablations: N/A (no experiments, hence no ablations). The analytical equivalent is Table 1, which decomposes which research directions address which challenges, and the two-way framing (CBR-for-LLM vs LLM-for-CBR) clarifying which integration lever targets which weakness.
evaluation_decoupling: N/A (no evaluation conducted). It does argue conceptually for transparent retrieval whose case-similarity decisions are inspectable (explaining which features/attributes drove a retrieval), i.e. a qualitative interest in the retrieval step's quality separate from final output, but reports no intrinsic-vs-end-to-end metric split.
process_vs_outcome_metrics: N/A (no metrics). Conceptually the manifesto stresses process transparency: explainable, similarity-based retrieval decisions and reasoning traces (turning structured cases/reasoning traces into human-readable explanations), reflecting interest in process quality beyond final-answer correctness -- but nothing is measured.
cost_efficiency_tradeoff: Discussed qualitatively as a core theme (Operational Efficiency). Challenges: high computational complexity/size of LLMs (C9), context-window limits and large serialized structured inputs increasing input size, latency, and inference cost (C2). Proposed efficiency directions: case-based distillation of LLMs (O5.1), fine-tuning smaller models on structured cases to speed inference (O5.2), and efficient case selection extracting only critical facts within limited context windows with adaptive similarity thresholds (O5.4). No quantitative cost/latency numbers are reported by the paper.
context_budget_and_selection_count: Discussed conceptually rather than numerically: context-window limitation is a named challenge (C2 -- structured serializations bloat tokens, cost, and latency), and the proposed lever is precision-/budget-driven efficient case selection that extracts critical facts and dynamically adjusts similarity thresholds to fit within limited LLM context windows (O5.4). No fixed k or token budget is prescribed.
survey_scope_and_axes: Explicit organizing axes: (1) two top-level research directions -- CBR-for-LLM (improving LLM utility) and LLM-for-CBR (LLMs supporting/advancing CBR); (2) four thematic research areas -- Guided Generation, Accuracy & Dehallucination, Explainability & Trust, Operational Efficiency; (3) CBR's four knowledge containers (vocabulary, similarity, case base, adaptation) and the 4R cycle (Retrieve/Reuse/Revise/Retain) as the mapping frame onto LLM mechanisms (episodic memory, case-based RAG, case-based planning); (4) a foundations section (case-based memory, knowledge structures, case-based retrieval, LLM-based knowledge acquisition/maintainability/explainability). Coverage: 13 challenges, 17 research directions, ~32 references; recent-window literature review (predominantly 2023-2025 works alongside foundational CBR references from the 1980s-2010s).
benchmark_construction_and_size: N/A (not a benchmark paper; constructs no dataset).
builds_on: Foundational CBR: Aamodt & Plaza 1994 (4R cycle, ref 1); Richter's knowledge containers (refs 26-27); Schank's Dynamic Memory Theory / MOPs (ref 29); Hammond's Case-Based Planning (ref 10); Hanney & Keane adaptation-knowledge bottleneck (ref 11); Munoz-Avila & Cox case-based plan adaptation (ref 23); Watson 1999 (CBR methodology, ref 33); Bergmann et al. CBR for planning (ref 3); process-oriented CBR (refs 20/22). LLM/RAG side: Lewis et al. RAG (ref 16/18); the 'episodic memory is the missing piece for long-term LLM agents' position (Pink et al. 2025, ref 24); DSPy (Khattab et al., ref 14); the Prompt Report (ref 30); LLM-Modulo / 'LLMs Can't Plan but can help planning' (Kambhampati et al.); MetaGPT (ref 12); structured-output works (refs 17-19). Companion CBR-LLM systems: CBR-RAG (Wiratunga et al. 2024, ref 35), Wilkerson & Leake (implementing CBR with LLMs, ref 34), Brand et al. (LLMs as Knowledge Engineers, ref 4), DS-Agent (Guo et al. 2024, ref 9), CBR-Ren (Feng et al., ref 7), iSee platform (Caro-Martinez et al., ref 5).
contrasts_with: Contrasts hybrid CBR+LLM systems against the limitations of each pure paradigm: standalone LLMs (limited/no long-term memory, opaqueness/black-box, hallucination, non-deterministic outputs, context-window limits, high compute) and standalone classical CBR (knowledge-acquisition bottleneck, cold-start problem, limited cross-domain transferability of 4R algorithms). Also contrasts case-based RAG against plain RAG, arguing standard RAG retrieves overly broad/generic context whereas structured multi-level case comparison yields higher precision/specificity. Echoes the LLM-Modulo stance that LLMs can't plan alone but can help within structured frameworks.
lineage: Surveys / position papers lineage (Group: Surveys). It is a community manifesto sitting at the CBR <-> LLM intersection, downstream of foundational CBR (Aamodt & Plaza, Richter, Schank, Hammond) and of the RAG/agentic-LLM lineage, and serving as an umbrella that frames and motivates the concrete CBR-LLM works in this collection (e.g. CBR-RAG, case-based planning, episodic-memory agents, structured-output de-hallucination). Companion follow-ups elaborate its themes (e.g. Leake et al.'s 'Levels of AI Memory' extends its memory opportunities). Distinct from generic RAG surveys (e.g. Gao et al.) by being explicitly CBR-grounded and bidirectional (CBR-for-LLM and LLM-for-CBR).
